newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil TAM's future seen hinging on accident cause.
newsitem.headline: Brazil TAM's future seen hinging on accident cause.

text.p: Brazilian airline TAM will experience a setback, the extent of which depends on the outcome of an investigation establishing the cause for Wednesday's accident, analysts said.

The accident, in which one passenger was killed and six others injured, came only eight months after another TAM aircraft ploughed into houses in a densely populated area of Sao Paulo, killing 98 people.

"Passenger numbers and financial results were already suffering after last year's disaster and with this new accident the firm's image is bound to suffer even more, even though the cause is not yet known," said Irineu Luiz Correa Filho, an analyst at Lopes Filho consulting firm.

The Ministry of Aviation and the Federal Police are investigating whether a bomb caused the explosion at the back of the TAM aircraft which tore a hole in the fuselage and forced an emergency landing at Sao Paulo's domestic airport.

"Everything depends on whether it was a bomb or not," Filho said. "If it turns out to be a maintenance fault, the consequences for the company would be serious. If it was a bomb, it will have a negative effect on all Brazilian airlines."
Analysts also said TAM's finances could suffer severely if it did turn out that a bomb caused the accident, as insurance generally does not cover that kind of event.

TAM, the fastest growing carrier in Latin America, currently transports over four million passengers a year. Airline officials said passenger movement Thursday was normal and no fall in numbers had been seen.
TAM specializes in business travel in Brazil and the Mercosur trade bloc, which is comprised of Paraguay, Uruguay, Argentina and Brazil.
The company uses a fleet of Fokker-100 aircraft which require only low maintenance, and have contributed to the firm's high profitability.

TAM also announced last year it would start non-stop flights between Brazil and the United States, and between major Brazilian state capitals in the second half of 1997. Recently, TAM signed a code-sharing agreement with American Airlines.

The airline has seen revenues jump 74 percent since 1994 to an estimated $650 million this year, and its number of passengers surge 186 percent since 1994 to a projected 4.7 million this year. It was recently voted company of the year by Brazil's business magazine Exame.
But a U.S. agency only last week gave TAM a low safety rating, while Brazil's Department of Civil Aviation (DAC) has reprimanded and fined the company a number of times this year for safety matters.
TAM's preferred stock took a beating today on the Sao Paulo Stock exchange, with the shares sliding 11.72 percent by mid-afternoon to 56.50 reais.
